167: def format_array_flat(array, max_width: int):
168:     """Return a formatted string for as many items in the flattened version of
169:     array that will fit within max_width characters.
170:     """
171:     # every item will take up at least two characters, but we always want to
172:     # print at least first and last items
173:     max_possibly_relevant = min(
174:         max(array.size, 1), max(int(np.ceil(max_width / 2.0)), 2)
175:     )
176:     relevant_front_items = format_items(
177:         first_n_items(array, (max_possibly_relevant + 1) // 2)
178:     )
179:     relevant_back_items = format_items(last_n_items(array, max_possibly_relevant // 2))
180:     # interleave relevant front and back items:
181:     #     [a, b, c] and [y, z] -> [a, z, b, y, c]
182:     relevant_items = sum(
183:         zip_longest(relevant_front_items, reversed(relevant_back_items)), ()
184:     )[:max_possibly_relevant]

186:     cum_len = np.cumsum([len(s) + 1 for s in relevant_items]) - 1
187:     if (array.size > 2) and (
188:         (max_possibly_relevant < array.size) or (cum_len > max_width).any()

191:         count = min(
192:             array.size, max(np.argmax(cum_len + len(padding) - 1 > max_width), 2)
193:         )
194:     else:
195:         count = array.size
196:         padding = "" if (count <= 1) else " "
197: 
198:     num_front = (count + 1) // 2
199:     num_back = count - num_front
200:     # note that num_back is 0 <--> array.size is 0 or 1
201:     #                         <--> relevant_back_items is []
202:     pprint_str = "".join(
203:         [
204:             " ".join(relevant_front_items[:num_front]),
205:             padding,
206:             " ".join(relevant_back_items[-num_back:]),
207:         ]
208:     )
209: 
210:     # As a final check, if it's still too long even with the limit in values,
211:     # replace the end with an ellipsis
212:     # NB: this will still returns a full 3-character ellipsis when max_width < 3
213:     if len(pprint_str) > max_width:
214:         pprint_str = pprint_str[: max(max_width - 3, 0)] + "..."

454:     obj: DataArray | Dataset, coords: Mapping[Any, Variable]
455: ) -> None:

458:     obj: DataArray or Dataset

answer_sentences.text: The `type_check` error block reporting that relative import paths need explicit file extensions in ECMAScript imports is located at `src/index.ts` on lines 1 and 2, which is causing the build to fail in the CI pipeline.

Specifically, line 1 shows error `TS2835` for the import of `./app`, and line 2 shows the same error for `./router`, both indicating that under `'moduleResolution': 'node16'`, these imports must use explicit `.js` extensions like `./app.js` and `./router.js`.

HOW_TO_RELEASE:1:How to issue an xarray release in 15 easy steps
HOW_TO_RELEASE:2:
HOW_TO_RELEASE:3:Time required: about an hour.
HOW_TO_RELEASE:4:
HOW_TO_RELEASE:5: 1. Ensure your master branch is synced to upstream:
HOW_TO_RELEASE:6:       git pull upstream master
HOW_TO_RELEASE:7: 2. Look over whats-new.rst and the docs. Make sure "What's New" is complete
HOW_TO_RELEASE:8:    (check the date!) and consider adding a brief summary note describing the
HOW_TO_RELEASE:9:    release at the top.
HOW_TO_RELEASE:10:    Things to watch out for:
HOW_TO_RELEASE:11:    - Important new features should be highlighted towards the top.
HOW_TO_RELEASE:12:    - Function/method references should include links to the API docs.
HOW_TO_RELEASE:13:    - Sometimes notes get added in the wrong section of whats-new, typically
HOW_TO_RELEASE:14:      due to a bad merge. Check for these before a release by using git diff,
HOW_TO_RELEASE:15:      e.g., ``git diff v0.X.Y whats-new.rst`` where 0.X.Y is the previous
HOW_TO_RELEASE:16:      release.
HOW_TO_RELEASE:17: 3. If you have any doubts, run the full test suite one final time!
HOW_TO_RELEASE:18:      py.test
HOW_TO_RELEASE:19: 4. On the master branch, commit the release in git:
HOW_TO_RELEASE:20:      git commit -a -m 'Release v0.X.Y'
HOW_TO_RELEASE:21: 5. Tag the release:
HOW_TO_RELEASE:22:      git tag -a v0.X.Y -m 'v0.X.Y'
HOW_TO_RELEASE:23: 6. Build source and binary wheels for pypi:
HOW_TO_RELEASE:24:      git clean -xdf  # this deletes all uncommited changes!
HOW_TO_RELEASE:25:      python setup.py bdist_wheel sdist
HOW_TO_RELEASE:26: 7. Use twine to register and upload the release on pypi. Be careful, you can't
HOW_TO_RELEASE:27:    take this back!
HOW_TO_RELEASE:28:      twine upload dist/xarray-0.X.Y*
HOW_TO_RELEASE:29:    You will need to be listed as a package owner at
HOW_TO_RELEASE:30:    https://pypi.python.org/pypi/xarray for this to work.
HOW_TO_RELEASE:31: 8. Push your changes to master:
HOW_TO_RELEASE:32:      git push upstream master
HOW_TO_RELEASE:33:      git push upstream --tags
HOW_TO_RELEASE:34: 9. Update the stable branch (used by ReadTheDocs) and switch back to master:
HOW_TO_RELEASE:35:      git checkout stable
HOW_TO_RELEASE:36:      git rebase master
HOW_TO_RELEASE:37:      git push upstream stable
HOW_TO_RELEASE:38:      git checkout master
HOW_TO_RELEASE:39:    It's OK to force push to 'stable' if necessary.
HOW_TO_RELEASE:40:    We also update the stable branch with `git cherrypick` for documentation
HOW_TO_RELEASE:41:    only fixes that apply the current released version.
HOW_TO_RELEASE:42:10. Add a section for the next release (v.X.(Y+1)) to doc/whats-new.rst.
HOW_TO_RELEASE:43:11. Commit your changes and push to master again:
HOW_TO_RELEASE:44:      git commit -a -m 'Revert to dev version'
HOW_TO_RELEASE:45:      git push upstream master
HOW_TO_RELEASE:46:    You're done pushing to master!
HOW_TO_RELEASE:47:12. Issue the release on GitHub. Click on "Draft a new release" at
HOW_TO_RELEASE:48:    https://github.com/pydata/xarray/releases. Type in the version number, but
HOW_TO_RELEASE:49:    don't bother to describe it -- we maintain that on the docs instead.
HOW_TO_RELEASE:50:13. Update the docs. Login to https://readthedocs.org/projects/xray/versions/
HOW_TO_RELEASE:51:    and switch your new release tag (at the bottom) from "Inactive" to "Active".
HOW_TO_RELEASE:52:    It should now build automatically.
HOW_TO_RELEASE:53:14. Issue the release announcement! For bug fix releases, I usually only email
HOW_TO_RELEASE:54:    xarray@googlegroups.com. For major/feature releases, I will email a broader
HOW_TO_RELEASE:55:    list (no more than once every 3-6 months):
HOW_TO_RELEASE:56:      pydata@googlegroups.com, xarray@googlegroups.com,
HOW_TO_RELEASE:57:      numpy-discussion@scipy.org, scipy-user@scipy.org,
HOW_TO_RELEASE:58:      pyaos@lists.johnny-lin.com
HOW_TO_RELEASE:59:    Google search will turn up examples of prior release announcements (look for
HOW_TO_RELEASE:60:    "ANN xarray").
HOW_TO_RELEASE:61:
HOW_TO_RELEASE:62:Note on version numbering:
HOW_TO_RELEASE:63:
HOW_TO_RELEASE:64:We follow a rough approximation of semantic version. Only major releases (0.X.0)
HOW_TO_RELEASE:65:show include breaking changes. Minor releases (0.X.Y) are for bug fixes and
HOW_TO_RELEASE:66:backwards compatible new features, but if a sufficient number of new features
HOW_TO_RELEASE:67:have arrived we will issue a major release even if there are no compatibility
HOW_TO_RELEASE:68:breaks.
HOW_TO_RELEASE:69:
HOW_TO_RELEASE:70:Once the project reaches a sufficient level of maturity for a 1.0.0 release, we
HOW_TO_RELEASE:71:intend to follow semantic versioning more strictly.

114:     without requiring an application object ahead of time. It uses the
115:     same decorators as :class:`~flask.Flask`, but defers the need for an
116:     application by recording them for later registration.

119:     that is called with :class:`~flask.blueprints.BlueprintSetupState`
120:     when the blueprint is registered on an application.

42:     """Group an array by its unique values.

44:     Parameters

57:         the corresponding value in `unique_values`.

172: def decode_cf_datetime(num_dates, units, calendar=None, use_cftime=None):

177:     operations, which makes it much faster than cftime.num2date. In such a
178:     case, the returned array will be of type np.datetime64.

181:     not larger than days.

185:     cftime.num2date

207:                         "numpy.datetime64 objects, continuing using "
208:                         "cftime.datetime objects instead, reason: dates out "
209:                         "of range",
210:                         SerializationWarning,
211:                         stacklevel=3,
212:                     )

214:                 if calendar in _STANDARD_CALENDARS:
215:                     dates = cftime_to_nptime(dates)

272: def infer_datetime_units(dates):
273:     """Given an array of datetimes, returns a CF compatible time-unit string of
274:     the form "{time_unit} since {date[0]}", where `time_unit` is 'days',
275:     'hours', 'minutes' or 'seconds' (the first one that can evenly divide all
276:     unique time deltas in `dates`)

278:     dates = np.asarray(dates).ravel()
279:     if np.asarray(dates).dtype == "datetime64[ns]":
280:         dates = to_datetime_unboxed(dates)

286:         reference_date = format_cftime_datetime(reference_date)

291:         unique_timedeltas = to_timedelta_unboxed(unique_timedeltas)

322: def cftime_to_nptime(times):
323:     """Given an array of cftime.datetime objects, return an array of
324:     numpy.datetime64 objects of the same size"""
325:     times = np.asarray(times)
326:     new = np.empty(times.shape, dtype="M8[ns]")
327:     for i, t in np.ndenumerate(times):
328:         try:
329:             # Use pandas.Timestamp in place of datetime.datetime, because
330:             # NumPy casts it safely it np.datetime64[ns] for dates outside
331:             # 1678 to 2262 (this is not currently the case for
332:             # datetime.datetime).
333:             dt = pd.Timestamp(
334:                 t.year, t.month, t.day, t.hour, t.minute, t.second, t.microsecond
335:             )
336:         except ValueError as e:
337:             raise ValueError(
338:                 "Cannot convert date {} to a date in the "
339:                 "standard calendar.  Reason: {}.".format(t, e)
340:             )
341:         new[i] = np.datetime64(dt)
342:     return new

355: def _encode_datetime_with_cftime(dates, units, calendar):
356:     """Fallback method for encoding dates using cftime.
357: 
358:     This method is more flexible than xarray's parsing using datetime64[ns]
359:     arrays but also slower because it loops over each element.

364:         # numpy's broken datetime conversion only works for us precision

367:     def encode_datetime(d):
368:         return np.nan if d is None else cftime.date2num(d, units, calendar)
369: 
370:     return np.vectorize(encode_datetime)(dates)

380: def encode_cf_datetime(dates, units=None, calendar=None):
381:     """Given an array of datetime objects, returns the tuple `(num, units,
382:     calendar)` suitable for a CF compliant time variable.
383: 
384:     Unlike `date2num`, this function can handle datetime64 arrays.
385: 
386:     See also
387:     --------
388:     cftime.date2num
389:     """

391: 
392:     if units is None:
393:         units = infer_datetime_units(dates)
394:     else:
395:         units = _cleanup_netcdf_time_units(units)

397:     if calendar is None:
398:         calendar = infer_calendar_name(dates)
399: 
400:     delta, ref_date = _unpack_netcdf_time_units(units)
401:     try:
402:         if calendar not in _STANDARD_CALENDARS or dates.dtype.kind == "O":
403:             # parse with cftime instead
404:             raise OutOfBoundsDatetime
405:         assert dates.dtype == "datetime64[ns]"
406: 
407:         delta_units = _netcdf_to_numpy_timeunit(delta)
408:         time_delta = np.timedelta64(1, delta_units).astype("timedelta64[ns]")
409:         ref_date = pd.Timestamp(ref_date)
410: 
411:         # If the ref_date Timestamp is timezone-aware, convert to UTC and
412:         # make it timezone-naive (GH 2649).
413:         if ref_date.tz is not None:
414:             ref_date = ref_date.tz_convert(None)
415: 
416:         # Wrap the dates in a DatetimeIndex to do the subtraction to ensure
417:         # an OverflowError is raised if the ref_date is too far away from
418:         # dates to be encoded (GH 2272).
419:         num = (pd.DatetimeIndex(dates.ravel()) - ref_date) / time_delta
420:         num = num.values.reshape(dates.shape)
421: 
422:     except (OutOfBoundsDatetime, OverflowError):
423:         num = _encode_datetime_with_cftime(dates, units, calendar)
424: 
425:     num = cast_to_int_if_safe(num)
426:     return (num, units, calendar)

429: def encode_cf_timedelta(timedeltas, units=None):
430:     if units is None:
431:         units = infer_timedelta_units(timedeltas)
432: 
433:     np_unit = _netcdf_to_numpy_timeunit(units)
434:     num = 1.0 * timedeltas / np.timedelta64(1, np_unit)
435:     num = np.where(pd.isnull(timedeltas), np.nan, num)
436:     num = cast_to_int_if_safe(num)
437:     return (num, units)
